¶
'''water-yam''' (wâ′tėr-yam), ''n.'' The latticeleaf; either of the plants ''Aponogeton'' (''Ouvirandra'') ''fenestralis'' and ''A.'' (''O.'') ''Berneriana:'' so called from its aquatic growth and farinaceous rootstock. See ''latticeleaf'' and ''Ouvirandra''.

'''water-yarrow''' (wâ′tėr-yãr″ō), ''n.'' The water-violet, ''Hottonia palustris:'' so called from its leaves being finely divided like those of yarrow. ''Britten and Holland.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''wath†''', ''n.'' [< Icel. ''vadh'' = Sw. ''vad'', a ford: see ''wade'', ''n.''] A ford. ''Halliwell.''

'''wathe<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' [< ME. ''wathe'' (also, after Icel., ''waith'', ''wayth''), < AS. ''wāth'', ''wǣth'', hunting, game, = OHG. ''weida'', MHG. G. ''weide'', pasture, meadow, = Icel. ''veidhr'', hunting, fishing. Cf. ''gain''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' The pursuit of game; hunting.
{{smaller block|<poem>“ȝe, we ar in wudlond,” cothe the king, “and walkes on owre ''wayth'',
For to hunte atte the herd, with houunde and with horne.”</poem>
{{right|''Anturs of Arthur'' (ed. Robson), xxxiv.}}}}
'''2.''' Game; prey.
{{smaller block|Bi-fore alle the folk on the flette, frekez he beddez}}

'''wathe<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' [< ME. ''wathe'', ''wothe'', < Icel. ''vādhi'', danger, injury.] Peril; harm; danger.
{{smaller block|<poem>Trwe mon trwe restore,
Thenne thar [need] mon drede no ''wathe.''</poem>
{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2355.}}
He vnwoundit, I-wis, out of ''wothe'' paste.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 10696.}}}}

'''wathely†''', ''adv.'' [ME., < ''wathe''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] Dangerously; severely.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ector done was to dethe, & his day past,
Achilles woundit full ''wothely'' in were of his lyffe.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 8827.}}
<poem>Wroghte wayes fulle wyde, werrayande knyghtez,
And wondes alle ''wathely'', that in the waye stondez!</poem>
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2090.}}}}

'''Watling street.''' [< ME. ''Watlinge-strete'', < AS. ''Wætlinga stræt'', lit. the Watlings’ street: ''Wætlinga'', gen. pl. of ''Wætling'', a descendant of Wætla (< ''Wætla'', a man’s name, + ''-ing''<sup>3</sup>); ''stræt'', a road, street.] '''1.''' A celebrated Roman road leading from London (and possibly from Dover) northwestward across Britain. Hence —'''2†.''' The Milky Way, the ordinary name of which implies that it is a road.

'''watt''' (wot), ''n.'' [So called from the Scottish engineer and inventor James ''Watt'' (1736–1819).] The practical unit of electrical activity or power. {{smaller|The watt is equal to 10<sup>7</sup> ergs per second, or the same number of absolute c. g. s. units of electrical activity; or it is the rate of working in a circuit when the E. M. F. is one volt and the current one ampere. One horse-power is equal to 746 watts.}}

'''watte†''', ''n.'' See ''wat''<sup>3</sup>.

'''Watteau back.''' In ''dressmaking'', an arrangement of the back of a woman’s dress in which broad folds or plaits hang from the neck to the bottom of the skirt without interruption; by extension, any loose back to a dress, not girded at the waist. See cut under ''sack.''

'''Watteau bodice.''' A bodice of a woman’s dress having a square opening at the neck, and presenting some resemblance to the costumes in the paintings by the artist Watteau (beginning of the eighteenth century).

'''Watteau mantle.''' See ''mantle.''

'''wattle''' (wot′l), ''n.'' [Also dial. ''waddle''; < ME. ''watel'', < AS. ''watel'', ''watul'', a hurdle, in pl. twigs, thatching, tiles; cf. Bav. ''wadel'', twigs, fir-branches, Swiss ''wedele'', a bundle of twigs; perhaps akin to ''withy'', ''weed''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''wallet.''] '''1.''' A framework made of interwoven rods or twigs; a hurdle. See ''hurdle.''
{{smaller block|The walls are ''wattles'', and the covering leaves.
{{right|''Scott'', The Poacher.}}}}

See cuts under ''buffle'', ''grebe'', and ''Tachybaptes''.—'''4.''' The stormy petrel, or Mother Carey’s chicken. See cut under ''petrel''.

¶'''water-withe''' (wâ′tėr-with), ''n.'' A species of vine, ''Vitis Caribæa'', which grows in the West Indies in parched districts. {{smaller|It is so full of clear sap or water that a piece of the stem two or three yards long is said to afford a plentiful draught.}}

'''water-wood''' (wâ′tėr-wu̇d), ''n.'' A large rubiaceous tree, ''Chimarrhis cymosa'', of river-banks in the West Indies.

'''waterwork''' (wâ′tėr-wėrk), ''n.'' '''1.''' A structure, contrivance, or engine for conducting, distributing, or otherwise disposing of water: now commonly in the plural. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') An edifice with machinery constructed in London in 1594-5 for forcing up and conveying the water of the Thames to various parts of the city.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Titus, the brave and valorous young gallant,
Three years together in the town hath been,
Yet my Lord Chancellor’s tomb he hath not seen,
Nor the new ''waterwork''.</poem>
{{right|''Sir J. Davies'' (?), Epigrams (1596), vi., In Titum.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Mam.'' Shall serve the whole city with preservative
Weekly; each house his dose, and, at the rate—
''Sur.'' As he that built the ''waterwork'' doth with water.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Alchemist, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') [In plural form, as ''sing.'' or ''pl.''] The aggregate of constructions and appliances for the collection, preservation, and distribution of water for domestic purposes, for the working of machinery, or otherwise for the use of a community. (''c'') An appliance through which water is spouted out in jets, sprays, or showers; a fountain; a hydraulic toy.}}

{{smaller block|Some [gardens] are beautified with basons of water in open pavilions, or with fountains and little ''water works'', in which, and their pleasant summer houses, their chief beauty consists. {{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. i. 123.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') ''pl.'' Same as ''tear-pump.'' [Humorous slang.]}}
{{smaller block|Sneaking little brute, . . . clapping on the ''waterworks'' just in the hardest place.
{{right|''T. Hughes'', Tom Brown at Rugby, ii. 5.}}}}
'''2†.''' A marine scene or pageant.
{{smaller block|The first scæne is a ''water-worke'' presented by Oceanus, king of the sea.
{{right|''Dekker'', Londons Tempe (Works, ed. Pearson, IV. 118).}}}}
{{smaller block|[In the following quotation the word is used punningly, with reference to the freezing over of the Thames during the winter of 1607-8.}}
{{smaller block|''Coun.'' Make me so much beholding to you as to receive from you the right picture of all these your ''water works''. . . .
''Cit.'' The Thames began to put on his “freeze-coat,” which he yet wears, about the week before Christmas; and hath kept it on till now this latter end of January.
{{right|''The Great Frost'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 83).]}}}}
'''3†.''' Painting with water or something soluble in water as a vehicle.—'''4.''' Hence, a textile fabric, as canvas, painted in this manner, and used instead of tapestry to decorate apartments.
{{smaller block|The king for himself had a house of timber, . . . and for his other lodgings he had great and goodlie tents of blew ''water-worke'', garnished with yellow and white.
{{right|''Holinshed'', Chronicle, III. 819.}}}}
{{smaller block|For thy walls, a pretty slight drollery, . . . or the German hunting in ''water-work'', is worth a thousand of these bed-hangings, and these fly-bitten tapestries.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., ii. 1. 158.}}}}

'''water-worker''' (wâ′tėr-wėr″kėr), ''n.'' One whose work has to do with water; in provincial English use, a maker of meadow-drains and wet ditches.   ''Halliwell.''

'''water-worm''' (wâ′tėr-wėrm), ''n.'' A water annelid, as a naidid.

'''water-worn''' (wâ′tėr-wōrn), ''a.'' Worn by the action of water; especially, smoothed by the force or action of running water, or water in motion: as, ''water-worn'' pebbles.

'''waterwort''' (wâ′tėr-wėrt), ''n.'' '''1.''' A plant of the genus ''Elatine'', or more broadly of the order ''Elatinaceæ'', primarily ''E. Hydropiper'' of the Old World.—'''2.''' The plant ''Philydrum lanuginosum'', or (Lindley) any plant of the order ''Philydraceæ''.

'''water-wraith''' (wâ′tėr-rāth), ''n.'' A supposed water-spirit, whose appearance prognosticates death or woe to the person seeing it.
{{smaller block|<poem>By this the storm grew loud apace;
The ''water-wraith'' was shrieking.</poem>
{{right|''Campbell'', Lord Ullin’s Daughter.}}}}

'''watery''' (wâ′tėr-i), ''a.''   [< ME. ''watery'', ''wateri'', ''watry'', ''watri'', < AS. ''wæterig'' (= D. ''waterig'' = MHG. ''wezzeric'', ''wazzeric'', G. ''wässerig''), < ''wæter'', water: see ''water''.]   '''1.''' Abounding in, moist with, or containing water; discharging water; wet; dripping; watered; specifically, of the eyes, tearful or running.
{{smaller block|<poem>“After sharpe shoures,” quod Pees, “moste shene is the sonne;
Is no weder warmer than after ''watery'' cloudes.”</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xviii. 410.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>This lady
Walks discontented, with her ''watery'' eyes
Bent on the earth.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid’s Tragedy, i. 1.}}}} '''2.''' Consisting of water.
{{smaller block|<poem>The queen o’ the sky,
Whose ''watery'' arch and messenger am I [Iris].</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1. 71.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Far off from these a slow and silent stream,
Lethe, the river of oblivion, rolls
Her ''watery'' labyrinth.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 584.}}}}
'''3.''' Resembling water; suggestive of water. {{smaller|(''a'') Thin, as a liquid; of slight consistency.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Nowe this vynes, whoso taketh kepe,
Not ''wattery'' but thicke humours wepe.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 104.}}}}
{{smaller|Hence—(''b'') Weak; vapid; insipid.}}
{{smaller block|The heorte, thet was ''wateri'', smecchles, and ne uelede no sauur of God.
{{right|''Ancren Riwle'', p. 376.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Slight Sir Robert with his ''watery'' smile.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Edwin Morris.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') Liquid; soft, and more or less transparent; pale.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The chasm in which the sun has sunk is shut, . . .
And over it a space of ''watery'' blue,
Which the keen evening star is shining through.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Evening.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Slant ''watery'' lights, from parting clouds, apace
Travel along the precipice’s base.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Evening Walk.}}}}
{{smaller|(''d'') Insipid and soft or flabby, as a fish or its flesh.}}
'''4.''' Pertaining to, connected with, or affecting water: specifically used of the moon, as governing the tide.
{{smaller block|<poem>Whiles winter frets the seas, and ''wat’ry'' Orion.</poem>
{{right|''Surrey'', Æneid, iv. 67.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>All springs reduce their currents to mine eyes,
That I, being govern’d by the ''watery'' moon,
May send forth plenteous tears to drown the world!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., ii. 2. 69.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''watery'' god</poem> Roll’d from a silver urn his crystal flood.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>What will it be,
When that the ''watery'' palate tastes indeed

{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., iii. 2. 22.}}}}

See ''star''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Watery fusion.''' See ''aqueous fusion'', under ''fusion''.—'''Watery itch,''' scabies attended with the formation of vesicles.}}

M. F. is one volt and the current one ampere. One horse-power is equal to 746 watts.}}

'''watte†''', ''n.'' See ''wat''<sup>3</sup>.

'''Watteau back.''' In ''dressmaking'', an arrangement of the back of a woman’s dress in which broad folds or plaits hang from the neck to the bottom of the skirt without interruption; by extension, any loose back to a dress, not girded at the waist. See cut under ''sack.''

'''Watteau bodice.''' A bodice of a woman’s dress having a square opening at the neck, and presenting some resemblance to the costumes in the paintings by the artist Watteau (beginning of the eighteenth century).

'''Watteau mantle.''' See ''mantle.''

'''wattle''' (wot′l), ''n.''   [Also dial. ''waddle''; < ME. ''watel'', < AS. ''watel'', ''watul'', a hurdle, in pl. twigs, thatching, tiles; cf. Bav. ''wadel'', twigs, fir-branches, Swiss ''wedele'', a bundle of twigs; perhaps akin to ''withy'', ''weed''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''wallet.'']   '''1.''' A framework made of interwoven rods or twigs; a hurdle. See ''hurdle.''
{{smaller block|The walls are ''wattles'', and the covering leaves.
{{right|''Scott'', The Poacher.}}}}

{{smaller block|They are gallant hares, and the scent lies thick right across another meadow, . . . and then over a good ''wattle'' with a ditch on the other side.
{{right|''T. Hughes'', Tom Brown at Rugby, i. 7.}}}}
'''2.''' A rod; a wand; a switch; a twig.
{{smaller block|A ''Wattle'', rod, vibex.
{{right|''Levins'', Manip. Vocab. (E. E. T. S.), p. 38.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Nae whip nor spur, but just a ''wattle''
O’ saugh or hazel.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', Farmer’s Salutation to his Auld Mare.}}}}
'''3†.''' A basket; a bag or wallet. ''Piers Plowman'' (C), xi. 269.—'''4.''' In ''ornith.'', a fleshy lobe hanging from the front of the head; specifically, such a lobe of the domestic hen, or a like formation of any bird. {{smaller|Wattles most properly so called are paired, as in the hen, but may be single, as the dewlap of the turkey. They are very various in size, shape, and color, but are usually pendent, and of some bright tint, as red, yellow, or blue. They occur in several different orders of birds, and among species whose near relatives are devoid of such appendages. Similar lobes or flaps on the auriculars are sometimes called ''ear-wattles'', though more properly ''ear-lobes''. See ''wattle-bird'', ''wattle-crow'', phrases under ''wattled'', and cuts under ''Gallus'' and ''Rasores''.}}
{{smaller block|The combs or ''wattles'' [of young gamecocks] are to be cut as soon as they appear; and the cock chickens are to be separated as soon as they begin to peck each other.
{{right|''J. Ashton'', Social Life in Reign of Queen Anne, I. 302.}}}}
'''5.''' A flap of skin forming a sort of dewlap on each side of the neck of some domestic swine.
{{smaller block|Y<sup>e</sup> ''Wattle'' of a hog, neuus.
{{right|''Levins'', Manip. Vocab. (E. E. T. S.), p. 38.}}}}
{{smaller block|Goitrons. Waddles, or ''wattles'', the two little and long excrescences which hang teat-like at either side of the throat of some hogs.
{{right|''Cotgrave'', 1611.}}}}
'''6.''' In ''ichth.'', a fleshy excrescence about the mouth; a barbel.

{{smaller block|The Barbel is so called, says Gesner, by reason of his barb or ''wattles'' at his mouth, which are under his nose or chaps.
{{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 166.}}}}
'''7.''' One of various Australian and Tasmanian acacias, valued to some extent for their wood and for their gum, but more for their bark, which is rich in tannin. {{smaller|For tanbark the most important species are ''Acacia decurrens'', or (if it is distinct from this, as appears to be the case) ''A. mollissima'', the common black wattle, also called ''green'' or ''feathered wattle'', and ''A. pycnantha'', the broad-leafed or golden wattle. The silver wattle, ''A. dealbata'', closely allied to the black wattle, is distinguished by the ashen color of its young foliage, and is a taller tree of moister ground. Its bark is inferior, but is considerably used for lighter leathers. Other species yielding tan-bark are ''A. saligna'' (''A. leiophylla''), the blackwood or lightwood, ''A. Melanoxylon'', the native hickory (''A. subporosa''), ''A. penninervis'', etc. Several wattles yield a gum resembling gum arabic, somewhat exported for use in cotton-printing as an adhesive, etc. The principal sources of this product are the black wattle, the broad-leafed wattle, and ''A. homolophylla''.}} '''8.''' In ''her.'', a wattle or dewlap used in a bearing. Compare ''wattled''.—{{smaller|'''African wattle''', a South African tree, ''Acacia Natalitia''.—'''Alpine wattle''', ''Acacia pravissima'', a shrub or small tree of the Victorian Alps.—'''Black wattle, feathered wattle, golden wattle, green wattle.''' See def. 7.—'''Prickly wattle''', ''Acacia juniperina'', an evergreen shrub of Australia and Tasmania.—'''Raspberry-jam wattle.''' Same as ''raspberry-jam tree''.—'''Savannah wattle''', two West Indian verbenaceous trees, ''Citharexylum quadrangulare'' and ''C. cinerea''.—'''Silver wattle.''' See def. 7.—'''Soap-pod wattle.''' Same as ''soapnut'', 2.—'''Varnish-wattle''', the Australian ''Acacia verniciflua''.—'''Wallaby wattle''', an Australian shrub,}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
